studies.title: The First And The Last
studies.meaning: The chapter opens by reporting glorification as something already done: everything in the heavens and the earth has glorified God. Then ownership, then two verbs held together, giving life and causing death, then power over everything. The third ayah gives four names in one line, arranged as two pairs that cancel each other's limits. First and Last close off both ends of time. Outer and Inner close off any position in depth. Commentators handle each pair as a single statement, since neither half works alone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a chapter whose second half presses a community to spend before it is too late. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The surah spends six lines describing God before it asks for anything at all, and the first request does not arrive until the seventh, so the scale of the one asking is established before the size of the ask is known.

keyTerms.note: The verb is in the perfect tense here, reporting the glorification as accomplished rather than as ongoing. Five chapters of the Quran open with this verb and they do not all use the same tense, which the grammarians discuss.
Two ordinary adjectives of sequence. Paired, they close off both ends of time so that nothing is left before or after, and the classical commentators read the pair as one statement rather than two.

One means manifest or uppermost, the other hidden or innermost. Together they remove any position from which something could be nearer or further, and the commentators decline to picture either of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in these years was a town of boundaries: garden walls, tribal quarters, treaties defining who stood where. Property was described by what it adjoined, and a person by whose protection they were under. Naming God with four words of position, and then making the four cancel every position, worked against the most basic way that world had of saying where anything was.
studies.didYouKnow: Five chapters of the Quran open by saying that what is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and they do not all use the same tense. Three put the verb in the perfect, reporting the act as done, and two put it in the imperfect, so that it reads as continuing. This chapter is one of the three.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The four names work by exhausting the alternatives rather than by describing a quality. Each pair leaves no third position, so the effect is that there is nowhere to stand outside what is being named. That is a different method from attributing knowledge or power, and the chapter uses it first. Everything the surah later asks about money and about delay is addressed to people who have just been told there is no outside to the arrangement.

crossReferences.why: Closes another of these chapters with a run of divine names and the same report that everything glorifies Him.
Expands the knowledge of all things into the keys of the unseen and a single falling leaf.
Defines God by denial in the same compressed way, at the shortest length the Quran uses.

studies.applyIt: Pick a single object in the room and say honestly where it came from, going back as far as you can before you run out of knowledge. Three or four steps is usually the limit. The chapter's first three lines are an argument about what lies past the point where your account stops, and the exercise puts that point in front of you.

studies.title: With You Wherever You Are
studies.meaning: The ayah moves from the largest scale to the nearest in one sentence. Creation in six days and settling on the Throne come first. Early scholars handled those phrases carefully, affirming the words and declining to picture them. Then four directions of traffic are listed: into the earth and out of it, down from the sky and up into it. The last clause collapses the distance entirely. He is with you wherever you are.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the opening of a surah whose second half urges a community to spend before it is too late. No particular occasion is reported for this ayah. It belongs to a run of six opening ayat that describe God with almost no instruction attached. So a listener is given the scale of the one addressing him. The first request arrives only in the seventh ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for entering something narrow, used elsewhere of a rope passing through a needle's eye. It suits seed, rain and burial equally, which is why the classical readers list all three.
A verb of going up by stages rather than rising all at once. The same root names a ladder and the night ascent, and it is used here of prayers, deeds and angels returning.

The ordinary preposition for company. Early scholars are unanimous that it names God's knowledge and presence rather than a location, and they note that the ayah supplies the reading itself by ending with seeing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in this ayah was visible from a Medinan doorway. Seed went into the ground and came up as barley. Water went down and the wadi ran. Smoke and birds went up. Farmers spoke about the earth swallowing and giving back. The words of the ayah come from farming, not from philosophy. A listener could check the first four clauses by walking outside, which is what makes the last one land.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah just before this one gives four divine names in a single line: the First, the Last, the Outermost and the Innermost. That set occurs nowhere else in the Quran. This ayah then does the same work as a story. It runs from the six days of creation to the person reading, and ends inside the room.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims that pull in opposite directions are held in one sentence: God is enthroned above creation, and God is with every person wherever they happen to be. The classical tradition refuses to resolve the tension by dropping either half. Transcendence is kept by the throne and by the six days; nearness is kept by the last clause and explained as knowledge rather than as place. The ayah ends with seeing, which is how the two are joined.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same nearness physical rather than spatial, measuring it against something inside the reader's own body.
Applies the same accompaniment to a specific scene, a small group talking privately with God counted among them.
Supplies the four names that this ayah then spells out as a movement from creation to the present moment.

studies.applyIt: Read the last clause of this ayah in the least sacred place you go this week: a supermarket queue, a waiting room, a traffic jam. The sentence says wherever, and the word has to be tested somewhere ordinary or it stays theoretical. Notice whether the place feels different afterwards, and do not force it if it does not.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth in six days, then rose above the Throne. He knows what goes into the ground and what comes out, what comes down from the sky and what goes up. He is with you wherever you are.

studies.title: He Slides The Night Into The Day
studies.meaning: Ownership is stated a second time, three lines after the first, and this time it is followed by a destination: to God all matters are returned. Then comes the image the chapter chooses for how that works. He slips the night into the day and the day into the night, and the verb describes something being inserted rather than exchanged. Nothing here is sudden. The line closes on knowledge of what the chests hold, which attaches the slow visible change outside to something slower and unseen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. These ayat complete the surah's opening description, which runs for six lines before the first instruction arrives. No specific occasion is reported for them. The community being addressed had grown quickly and contained people at every stage of commitment, which is why the chapter keeps pairing statements about God's knowledge with statements about what a person holds inside.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb, so nobody is named as bringing the matters back. The construction leaves the agent out, which makes the returning sound like something that happens rather than something arranged.

A verb for putting one thing inside another, used of threading a cord through a narrow opening. It describes the lengthening of days as insertion rather than as exchange, which is how the change actually looks.
A phrase for the inner contents of a person rather than for the heart as an organ. It occurs many times in the Quran and always follows a statement about knowledge or about seeing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was read off the sky. Prayer, travel and trade were set by sunrise, midday, sunset and the stars, and the gradual shortening of daylight through the year was something a caravan leader knew in his body. Nobody owned a clock. The change described in this ayah was not an abstraction but the thing that decided when you left and when you stopped.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for sliding night into day appears four times in the Quran, and in each of them it is paired with a second statement about knowledge or power rather than being left to stand alone. The image is evidently kept for arguments rather than for description, and this chapter follows that pattern exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a process nobody can watch happening beside a knowledge nobody can escape, and the join is the point. Days do not change length in a way you could catch in the act, and yet they change. Hearts are described the same way later in this chapter, hardening over long duration. Divine knowledge is therefore introduced as the thing that reads gradual change, which is the kind human beings are worst at noticing in themselves.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same insertion of night and day beside bringing the living out of the dead and back.
Repeats the same verb and pairs it with the sun and the moon running to a stated term.
Applies the logic of slow change to the heart, saying long duration hardened those who came before.

studies.applyIt: Look up the sunset time for today and for the same date last month. The difference will be small, and you will not have felt it happening. The ayah describes that exact process and then turns to what is inside a person, and holding the two together for a minute is most of what the passage is asking of you.

studies.title: Spend From What You Inherited
studies.meaning: The chapter's first instruction arrives after six lines of description, and it is two commands joined: believe, and spend. What follows redefines the property. Spend from that in which He has made you successors, so the money is described as something handed on to you rather than earned by you. The word covers inheritance and stewardship at once, and the commentators keep both senses. The reward is then attached to the two verbs together, believing and spending, as one condition rather than as two.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a community that had recently acquired wealth it never had in Mecca. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Many in Medina had arrived as emigrants with nothing and were now, within a few years, property owners, so the chapter addresses people for whom a possession was a recent and slightly unfamiliar thing to hold.

keyTerms.note: Found only here in the Quran. It comes from the root for succeeding someone, so what you hold is described as a position you have inherited rather than as a thing you own outright.

The ordinary verb for laying out money, not a technical term for a due. The chapter uses it repeatedly and never narrows it, which keeps the instruction general rather than turning it into a calculation.
A plain adjective of size. The chapter attaches a different adjective to the reward each time it names one, and the variation becomes noticeable when the lines are read close together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Arabia moved by inheritance in a very visible way. A man's herds, his palms and his debts passed to named heirs, and the whole town knew the sequence. Everyone could say whose land they were standing on a generation earlier. Describing your property as something you had been made successor to was not a metaphor for that audience; it was how they already described most of what they held.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for your relationship to your property occurs only here in the Quran. It is built on the same root as the word for a successor placed on the earth, used in the account of the first human being, so the chapter quietly puts your household goods and that appointment into the same grammar.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ownership is neither denied nor left alone. The passage leaves the property in your hands and changes its description, which changes what spending is: not a transfer out of what is yours but a use of what was passed through you. On that reading generosity becomes a matter of accuracy rather than of sacrifice. And the instruction is bound to belief in one sentence, so the chapter treats the two as one act seen from two sides.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with a deadline, spend before a day comes in which there is no bargaining.
Places the same command against a man asking for a delay at the moment of his own death.
Tells them to spend from the good of what they earned and of what was brought out of the earth.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you own that came to you rather than being bought: a gift, an inheritance, a hand-me-down, a job someone put you forward for. Hold it for a moment. Then give something away today, any amount, while that particular item is still in your mind. The ayah is asking for exactly that sequence.

studies.title: What Is The Matter With You
studies.meaning: The chapter changes voice and asks a question with an edge on it. What is wrong with you that you do not believe, while the Messenger is calling you and a pledge has already been taken from you. Commentators divide over which pledge is meant, some reading the covenant taken from all human beings before this life and others a specific undertaking given in Medina, and the classical works carry both. The sentence closes by making the pledge rest on their own claim: if you are believers.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The chapter is speaking to a mixed audience, some of it fully committed and some holding back, and the tone here is a rebuke addressed to the second group without naming anyone. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. The same construction opens a second rebuke three lines later, and the parallel is close enough that the two are usually read as a pair.

keyTerms.note: A circumstantial clause, which in Arabic sets the calling alongside the refusal as simultaneous. The grammar is what produces the sharpness, since it puts the invitation and the hesitation in the same moment.

A firm undertaking, from a root for binding something tightly. The ayah does not say which pledge, and the commentators list several, which is why the line reads as a reminder rather than as a citation.

The word is used at both ends of the ayah, once for what they are being called to and once for what they claim already to be. Putting the same term in both places is what turns the question into an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pledge in Arabia was physical and public. Men clasped hands, and the gesture bound a person in front of witnesses who would remember it for decades. Breaking one was the worst thing said about a man in poetry, worse than cowardice. An audience hearing that a pledge had already been taken from them would have understood the claim as something with a date and a place attached.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one three lines later open with the same two word construction, a rebuke that could be rendered what is the matter with you. The first is about believing and the second is about spending money. The chapter puts the two failures into identical grammar and never comments on the parallel it has made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question assumes the case has already been made and asks what is still holding the listener back. That is a different move from arguing, and it presumes two things: a call currently being issued, and a pledge already given. The passage therefore treats hesitation as a breach rather than as an open question, and it does so without specifying which pledge, which leaves the line usable by a reader who has made one of their own.

crossReferences.why: Reports the covenant taken from the descendants of Adam, one of the pledges the commentators name here.
Puts the same call in the mouths of those who answered it, a caller calling to belief and their reply.
Describes a pledge given in Medina with hands joined, and says the hand of God was above theirs.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made to yourself that you would recognise instantly if somebody read it back to you. Not a resolution; a real one, made at a specific moment. Say it out loud once today in the words you used at the time. The ayah's whole force comes from the pledge being already given, and most people have at least one.

studies.title: Out Of The Darknesses Into The Light
studies.meaning: The sending down is described by its purpose rather than by its content: clear signs, given to His servant, so that you may be brought out of darkness into light. The grammar is worth catching. Darkness is plural and light is singular, and the Quran keeps that pattern everywhere the phrase occurs. Then two names close the line and they are unusually gentle for a chapter that has been describing power. He is tender toward you, and merciful. The sending down is placed under those two words.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The line sits between two rebukes and softens the passage from inside it. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. The community it addresses had been receiving revelation in instalments for years by this point, so a description of clear signs coming down upon His servant was a description of something happening in their own street, not a general claim about scripture.

keyTerms.note: A plural. The Quran uses this phrase seven times and the plural never changes, so what is left behind is counted as many while what is arrived at is always one.
Singular and definite every time the phrase occurs. The contrast in number carries the meaning: ways of being lost are many, and the way out is not described as one among them.
A name for gentleness that avoids causing pain, which the lexicons distinguish from mercy by its attention to the small hurt. It is the softer of the two names here and is placed first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in a town without lamps was genuinely dark, and moving through it meant knowing the route by memory. A single lamp changed a room completely, and the oil for it was a real expense. The plural for darkness would have sounded natural to people who distinguished the dark of a moonless night from the dark of a covered alley and had a separate word for each.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about being brought out of darkness into light appears seven times in the Quran. In every one of them darkness is plural and light is singular, without exception, and the pattern holds even where the surrounding wording changes. Classical commentators notice it and read the plural as the many separate ways of going wrong.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described by its effect rather than by its status, which is a choice. What is sent is called clear signs, and the purpose given is extraction: being brought out, by someone, rather than finding your own way. The passive construction leaves the reader as the one moved. And the two names at the end make that movement an act of tenderness, an unexpected register in a chapter otherwise built on power and on settling accounts.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same movement and adds its reverse, those who take false patrons being led the other way.
Opens a surah by saying the Book was sent down for exactly this purpose, by their Lord's permission.
Repeats the phrase almost word for word, about a messenger reciting clear signs of God.

studies.applyIt: Turn off every light in one room tonight and sit for two minutes before switching a single one back on. Notice that the dark had textures and the light does not need any. That is the grammar of this ayah, plural on one side and singular on the other, and it is easier to feel in a room than to follow on a page.

studies.title: Before The Opening, And After
studies.meaning: The second rebuke matches the first and adds a reason: why do you not spend, when the inheritance of everything already belongs to God. Then a ranking is made openly. Those who spent and fought before the opening are not equal to those who did so afterwards; the first are greater in degree. And then the sentence turns, because both are promised the best. Commentators divide over whether the opening means the treaty made at Hudaybiyah or the entry into Mecca, and both readings are carried.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a moment when the community's position had changed enough that giving had become less risky than it once was. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah beyond that setting. Early supporters had given when the outcome was uncertain and the numbers small; later ones gave when the direction of events was becoming clear, and the ayah says plainly that the two are not the same.

keyTerms.note: The word for what passes to the heirs. Saying that the inheritance of the heavens and the earth belongs to God describes every holding as temporary by naming the party it reverts to.
A noun for opening something closed, used of a conquest and of a decisive judgement. Commentators read it as a specific turning point and divide over which one, and the classical works preserve both.
A superlative standing without a noun, so what is promised is left unnamed. It appears elsewhere for the reward of the righteous, and the vagueness is part of what makes it reassuring.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving when a cause is losing costs more than giving when it is winning, and everyone in that society could price the difference. Backing a weak party meant risking your standing with a strong one, and reputations were built on when a man committed rather than on whether he did. Poets recorded the timing of alliances precisely, because the timing was the honour.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the turning point is the title of another chapter, surah 48, which was revealed about a treaty rather than a battle. Commentators who connect the two read this ayah as ranking those who gave before that treaty, while others take it to mean the later entry into Mecca, and the classical works record both without deciding.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things that usually cancel each other are held inside one ayah. Ranks are real and are stated without softening, and then everyone in both ranks is promised the best. That combination is the chapter's characteristic move, and it does something specific to a reader: it removes the consolation that everyone is the same, and removes the despair that follows from being late, without letting either take over the sentence.

crossReferences.why: Names the foremost of the first and those who followed them well, and promises both God's pleasure.
Makes the same kind of distinction in rank while still promising the best to both groups named.
Returns to the loan made to God and its multiplication, this time with no ranking attached at all.

studies.applyIt: Find something you have been meaning to support and support it now, at whatever size, rather than when it becomes obviously worth supporting. The ayah's whole distinction is about timing rather than amount. It also promises the best to the late ones, which is worth holding on to if the line reads as an accusation rather than an invitation.

studies.title: Who Will Lend God A Loan
studies.meaning: A question is asked that nobody in the chapter answers. Who is the one who will lend God a good loan. The commentators spend time on the form of it, since the one asking owns everything already and needs nothing, and they read the wording as an invitation dressed as a request. The verb is the ordinary commercial one for lending. What is promised back is multiplication and then, separately, a generous reward, so the return and the reward are two things rather than one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a chapter urging a community with new wealth to spend it. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. The phrase it uses appears in six places in the Quran, in both Meccan and Medinan chapters, and two of those six are in this surah alone, seven lines apart, so the image was evidently familiar to the audience by the time it arrived here.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial verb for lending, from a root about cutting a piece off something. What you lend is cut from what you hold, so the word carries the sense of a portion separated and handed over.
An adjective describing the loan rather than the lender. Commentators explain it as given willingly, from what is good, and without looking to the person who received it for any return.
A verb of doubling repeatedly rather than once. The Quran uses it for the return on spending and states no fixed factor in this construction, which leaves the multiplication open-ended.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit ran the Arabian economy. Caravans were financed by lenders who took a share, debts were recorded and witnessed, and a man's ability to borrow depended entirely on whether he repaid. Everyone in the audience had been on both sides of a loan. The word chosen here is the one they used for that arrangement, with the single difference that the borrower is not short of anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about lending God a good loan appears six times in the Quran, and two of the six are in this chapter, seven lines apart. The first is a question with no answer supplied, and the second is a statement describing the people who answered it, so the surah poses and settles the same image within a single page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The image is deliberately uncomfortable. God is described as a borrower, which reverses every relation the chapter established in its first six lines, where everything already belongs to Him. The classical tradition reads the reversal as an accommodation to the listener rather than as a claim about need. What it does is change the feel of spending: money given is not gone but out on loan, which is a different thing to hold at the moment of handing it over.

crossReferences.why: Asks the identical question and adds that God straitens and expands, so the loan is not about need.
Makes the same offer and adds forgiveness to the multiplication as part of what comes back.
Places the loan beside prayer and charity as one of three things named at a surah's close.

studies.applyIt: Give something this week and deliberately do not think of it as gone. Not as a mental trick; as a description you are testing. The ayah offers you the word loan for that transaction, and the only way to find out whether it changes anything is to use it once, at the moment of giving, and see what it does.

studies.title: Their Light Running Ahead
studies.meaning: The scene is given as something you see rather than something you are told, and the light is what moves. It runs out in front of the believing men and women and at their right hands. Commentators read the light as their own deeds made visible, and note that it goes before them rather than trailing behind. The greeting that meets them is in the second person, so the reader is placed inside the group being congratulated. What is announced is gardens, permanence, and a word that means winning outright.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The chapter has been rebuking hesitation, and this is the reward side of the same argument, placed immediately before a scene of people who have no light at all. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. It names believing men and believing women separately, a construction the Medinan chapters use in passages about standing and about reward.

keyTerms.note: A verb of brisk movement used of a person hurrying somewhere. Applying it to light makes the light an agent rather than a property, and the commentators note that it goes ahead rather than being carried.
The plural of the word for a right hand, which in Arabic also carries good fortune. The light is placed forward and to one side, which is where a lamp held by somebody walking beside you would fall.
A noun for winning and for escaping at the same time, used of a prize and of a narrow deliverance. The Quran attaches it to this outcome repeatedly, and the adjective here is the chapter's largest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travelling at night in a group meant one or two lamps between many people, and whoever carried the light set the pace for everyone behind. Walking outside the circle of that light was how you got left behind. The picture in this ayah would have been familiar and slightly anxious to anyone who had made a night journey, which is most of the audience.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names believing men and believing women as two separate groups, and the chapter does the same in the next line for the other side. Both scenes are described twice over, once for each, which is a feature of a number of Medinan passages and is kept even where the description that follows is otherwise identical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reward is shown before it is explained, and what is shown is not a place but a condition: people with their own light, moving. That makes the outcome continuous with the life before it rather than a separate award, which is why the next ayah can describe others asking to borrow some of it. Light of that kind cannot be transferred, and the force of the following scene depends on the reader having accepted this one first.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of light running ahead and at the right hands, with a prayer to complete it.
Says that those who believe have their reward and their light, naming the same two things together.
Describes the arrival at the gates, with the greeting given in the same second person address.

studies.applyIt: Walk somewhere in the dark tonight with a torch and notice that the light arrives before you do. Every step is taken on ground the beam has already reached. The ayah chooses that detail specifically, and it is the kind of thing you have seen a thousand times without the seeing ever turning into a thought.

studies.title: Wait For Us, Let Us Borrow Light
studies.meaning: The request is the most human line in the chapter: wait for us, let us take something from your light. The verb is the one for lighting your own lamp from somebody else's flame, an ordinary neighbourly transaction. The answer sends them backwards, to look for light where light was earned, and then a wall goes up with a gate in it. Commentators note the strange geometry: mercy is on the inside and punishment on the outside, and one structure is described from two opposite directions.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a chapter addressing a community that contained people whose commitment was public and shallow. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Medina in this period had a recognisable group who attended, contributed occasionally and kept their options open, and the surah describes their position at the end rather than naming or accusing anybody in the present.

keyTerms.note: Found only here in the Quran. It is the exact word for carrying fire from a neighbour's hearth to light your own, which makes the request ordinary, reasonable and completely impossible in this setting.
The word for a city wall, a structure with a defined inside and outside. The Quran describes a barrier at this moment in more than one place, and this is the only one that gives the barrier a gate.

The same word used as a divine name in the chapter's third line, where it meant the Inner. Here it is architectural, so a reader meets the term twice in one surah in two completely different registers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire was borrowed constantly. Keeping a hearth alight through the night took fuel, and it was normal to send a child next door in the morning with a stick to bring back a flame. Refusing was almost unheard of, which is what makes the refusal in this ayah so unsettling: it denies a request nobody in that society would have turned down.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for borrowing light in this ayah occurs once in the Quran. It is the technical word for taking fire from another fire, and the same root gives Arabic its ordinary word for acquiring knowledge from a teacher, which the classical commentators mention when they explain the line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The scene turns on something that cannot be shared. Everything else in the chapter can be transferred, since money moves, support can be lent, and standing can be borrowed from a group. Light here cannot. That makes it a statement about what a person actually holds at the end: not their associations but the thing that was theirs from the start. The instruction to go back is the sharpest part, since it points at a place that no longer exists.

crossReferences.why: Describes another barrier on that day, with men on its heights who can see both sides at once.
Describes the same disposition in this life, standing for prayer lazily and to be seen by people.
Gives the scene these people are looking at, believers with their own light running ahead of them.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you do mainly because of who is watching. Everyone has one, and naming it is not a confession, it is an inventory. Then do that same thing once this week with nobody knowing. The ayah is about what is left when the company goes, and the only way to check is to remove the company briefly.

studies.title: Were We Not With You
studies.meaning: The question is fair on its face: were we not with you. The answer concedes it and then lists what being with someone is not. You put yourselves to the test, you waited, you doubted, and wishes deceived you until the command of God came. Four verbs in a row, which the commentators read as a sequence rather than a set, each one making the next easier. The line then names a deceiver, so the last word shifts the blame outward after four clauses of placing it firmly inward.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The exchange continues from the wall in the previous ayah and is the only extended dialogue in the chapter. No specific occasion is reported for it. Proximity was how belonging was measured in that society: you were with a group if you camped with it and turned out when it moved, and the claim being made here is exactly that claim, offered and refused.

keyTerms.note: The verb for testing metal in fire, here with the self as its object. Commentators read it as exposing yourselves to a trial you then failed, so the damage is described as self-inflicted before anything else is said.

keyTerms.gloss: and you waited, you held back
keyTerms.note: A verb for waiting to see how something turns out. It names a posture rather than an act, and it is the only item on this list that would have looked like prudence at the time.

The plural of a word for what you would like to be true, from a root for hoping. The Quran uses it of expectations held without ground, and here it is the agent of the sentence rather than its object.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting to see who won was a recognised strategy in Arabian politics and had a vocabulary of its own. Clans held back from an alliance until the outcome was visible and then joined the winner, and this was not thought shameful so much as shrewd. The chapter takes that ordinary caution and sets it in a list with doubt and self-deception, which is a reassessment rather than an accusation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the deceiver at the end of this ayah appears five times in the Quran, and two of the five are in this chapter, six lines apart. In the second the deceiving is done by worldly life itself, so the surah names the same effect twice over and gives it a different agent each time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes apart a claim that would stand up anywhere else. They were present, they were counted, and the answer says yes to all of it and still refuses the conclusion. What is named instead is a series of internal moves, none of them visible from outside, which is why nobody in the community could have sorted these people at the time. The chapter is describing something no human being is placed to adjudicate.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same waiting posture during life, watching to see which side an outcome will fall on.
Warns against the same deceiver by name, with the same warning about worldly life beside it.
Records what was said by those with sickness in their hearts at a moment of real pressure.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you are waiting to see the outcome of before committing to it. A cause, a relationship, a decision somebody else is making. Write down what you would do if you already knew how it turned out, and what you are doing now. The ayah lists waiting between doubt and self-deception, which is worth sitting with rather than agreeing to.

studies.title: No Ransom Will Be Taken
studies.meaning: The answer to the previous exchange ends with a refusal and then an inversion. No ransom is taken from you today, nor from those who openly refused, so the two groups are placed on one footing at the last moment. The Fire is called your shelter, using the word for the place you go home to, and then your protector, the word for the ally who stands behind you in a dispute. Both belong to the vocabulary of safety, and both are turned around inside a single line.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a passage about people whose commitment was visible but not real. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Ransom was a live institution: captives were exchanged for payment after a battle, families raised the sum, and the practice was recent enough in the audience's memory that denying it named a real and expected last resort.

keyTerms.note: A payment made to release someone, from a root about putting one thing in the place of another. What the line rules out is substitution itself rather than any particular price being too low.
The place a person goes at the end of a day, used of a home and of a resting place. The word normally carries safety, and applying it here removes the safety while keeping the finality.
A noun for where something ends up, from the verb for becoming. It closes many passages of the Quran and names the result of a process rather than a place that was chosen.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man without a patron in Arabia was exposed. Your clan answered for you, paid your blood money and took your side, and if you had none you found somebody to take you under their protection. Ransom worked the same way: after a defeat, relatives raised a payment and a captive came home. Both were how that society undid a disaster, and the ayah names them and cancels them.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the words in this short line come from the vocabulary of safety: a ransom that buys someone back, a shelter that takes someone in, and a patron who stands behind them. The ayah applies all three to the Fire without altering any of them, so the reversal is achieved entirely by placement rather than by reaching for harsher words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal of ransom makes the outcome personal in a way nothing else in the chapter does. Everything up to this point could be helped by somebody else: money is given, light is asked for, a group is joined. Here substitution is closed off in one clause. And the two words that follow describe the Fire in the language of belonging, which says that what a person ends with is what they were actually attached to.

crossReferences.why: Says the earth's weight in gold would not be accepted from those who died refusing, even if offered.
Imagines a man wanting to ransom himself with his children, his family and everyone on earth.
Denies both intercession and compensation on that day, in the same order this ayah uses.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last problem you solved with money that you could not have solved any other way. A repair, a fine, a fare home. Notice how normal that is, and how much of ordinary life runs on substitution. The whole weight of this ayah is in describing one situation where that mechanism is simply absent.

studies.title: Has The Time Not Come
studies.meaning: A question rather than an instruction, and the tone is close to remonstrance: has the time not yet come. What is asked for is a softening of hearts at the mention of God and at what has been sent down. Then a warning drawn from history: earlier communities were given a Book, the interval stretched out, and their hearts hardened. The mechanism named is duration. Nothing happened to them except that time passed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources agree, unusually, that this ayah was felt as a rebuke by the companions themselves. Several pass on that some of them said it came only a few years after their arrival in Medina. It follows a scene at the barrier, where the hypocrites ask for light. So the question put to believers arrives right after a picture of people who ran out of time.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning for a moment to ripen or fall due, used of fruit and of water reaching its boiling point. The question is about timing, not about capacity.
A verb used of ground going still and of eyes lowered. It describes a body settling rather than a feeling arriving, which is why the classical writers pair it with attentiveness in prayer.

keyTerms.gloss: the interval, the stretch of time
keyTerms.note: A word for a span with an endpoint, the distance between two markers. It names duration itself as the cause of hardening, without any event, which is what makes the warning uncomfortable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in these years was filling with people who had heard the Quran only recently. Others had carried it since Mecca. Wealth had arrived with the treaties and the growing territory. Houses that had been bare were now furnished. The ayah lands on a community for whom the emergency had eased. That is an exact and familiar moment in the life of any group under pressure.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the companions is reported to have said that only four years lay between the start of their belief and this ayah arriving to correct them. The report is kept in the major early collections. Whatever the exact gap, it is short. The warning about long time hardening a heart was delivered to people who had barely begun.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a way of failing that has nothing to do with disbelief or with any decision. Hearts harden on their own, from familiarity. The cure is not new information but fresh attention to what was already given. That puts the risk inside the community rather than outside it. It also puts it inside people who already believe. The ayah after this one answers with an image: God gives the earth life after its death.

crossReferences.why: Answers this warning immediately, offering a hardened heart the same treatment as dead ground.
Describes the same hardening with a mineral comparison, and notes that even rocks let water through.
Shows the opposite motion, bodies and hearts loosening at the same remembrance this ayah asks for.

studies.applyIt: Pick something in your practice that has gone automatic, and slow one instance of it down this week. Say the opening of a prayer at half speed. Read a passage you know by heart as if it arrived this morning. The ayah blames duration rather than intention, and the counter to duration is not effort but unfamiliarity.
studies.explainEasier: God asks believers whether it is not yet time for their hearts to soften. He means when they hear his name and what he sent down. He warns them not to be like earlier people who got a Book. Time went on, and their hearts got hard.

studies.title: The Earth After Its Death
studies.meaning: The instruction is to know something, and what follows is a fact about soil: God gives the earth life after its death. It arrives directly after a line about hearts hardening over long duration, so the commentators read it as the answer rather than as a new subject. Then the signs are said to be set out so that you may understand, and the passage returns to money. The men and women who give, and who have lent God a good loan, will have it multiplied and a generous reward besides.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. These two lines sit between a rebuke about hardened hearts and a statement about the truthful, and they carry the chapter's turn from warning back toward encouragement. No specific occasion is reported for them. Medina's agriculture depended on a short rainy window, so the revival of dead ground was an annual event the audience watched for rather than an image they had to imagine.

keyTerms.note: A plural imperative to know something. The chapter uses it twice within a few lines, and both times it introduces a fact meant to reframe what has just been said rather than to add information.
A form built on the root for giving alms, doubled to include both. The same root gives Arabic its words for truthfulness, which is why the next ayah can move to the truthful without changing subject.

A passive, where the question seven lines earlier used the active voice. The chapter asks who will lend and then reports the multiplication without naming who performs it, so the two lines do not repeat each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dead ground in Arabia looked genuinely dead: cracked, colourless, with nothing standing on it. After rain the change was fast enough to be startling, green showing within days on land that had held nothing for months. People walked out to look at it. That was the event the audience pictured, and it was seasonal, expected and still surprising every time.
studies.didYouKnow: The words for giving charity and for being truthful are built on the same Arabic root. This chapter uses one in a line about spending and the other in the line immediately after it, about the people it calls the deeply truthful, so two ayat that look like separate subjects are joined in the sound as well as in the sense.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A hardened heart is answered with a fact about ground rather than with an instruction. That places the remedy outside a person's own effort while leaving them responsible for noticing it, which is the balance the chapter keeps striking. Putting charity immediately afterwards is not a change of topic either, since giving is presented as what a softened heart does, so the spending the surah keeps asking for becomes a symptom rather than a duty.

crossReferences.why: Points at the traces of mercy reviving the earth and draws the same conclusion about reviving the dead.
Describes ground that is still and then stirs and swells when water is sent down on it.
States the problem this line answers, hearts hardened after a long interval had passed over them.

studies.applyIt: Water something that looks finished: a plant you gave up on, a patch of soil, a pot on a step. Do it for a week without expecting anything. The passage puts the revival of dead ground directly after a line about a heart gone hard, and it assumes you have watched the first before you think about the second.

studies.title: The Truthful And The Witnesses
studies.meaning: A rank is conferred rather than described. Those who believe in God and His messengers, these are the deeply truthful, and the witnesses with their Lord. Commentators divide over whether the second group is a separate rank or a continuation of the same sentence, and the classical works carry both readings. What is given them is two things, their reward and their light, and the light has been the chapter's own image since a few lines earlier. The opposite case is stated briefly and left without elaboration.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The line follows a passage about giving and precedes the parable of the withering crop, so it stands at the chapter's high point. No specific occasion is reported for it. The word translated as witnesses carries both the sense of giving testimony and of dying in a cause, and the classical commentators discuss both senses without settling on one.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth, describing someone whose truthfulness has become a characteristic rather than a series of acts. The Quran treats it as a named rank rather than as a compliment.
A plural covering those who testify and those who give their lives. Arabic holds both together, and the commentators let the ayah carry either, since seeing and being seen share one root.
The chapter has already shown this light running ahead of the believers and refused to others. Naming it here as something they possess ties the reward directly to that earlier scene.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the mechanism of Arabian justice. Without records a dispute was settled by who would stand up and say what they had seen, and a man known to be accurate was worth more in a quarrel than a document would have been. Reputations were built slowly and lost instantly. Naming a rank of the deeply truthful put a religious honour into the vocabulary of the courtroom.
studies.didYouKnow: Elsewhere the Quran gives four ranks in a single list: the prophets, the deeply truthful, the witnesses and the righteous. Two of those four are conferred here on anyone who believes in God and His messengers, which is why the classical commentators discuss at length whether the line is naming the same ranks or extending them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A rank normally associated with a few is attached to a condition anybody can meet. The classical tradition does not flatten the difference and it debates how much weight the word carries here, but the grammar of the sentence is plain. That places one of the highest descriptions in the Book within reach of belief itself, and the chapter balances it at once by turning to a parable about a crop that looked good and then yellowed.

crossReferences.why: Lists the four ranks, prophets, the truthful, the witnesses and the righteous, as company on the straight path.
Names the one who brought the truth and the one who confirmed it, calling them the God-conscious.
Shows the light these people are said to have, running ahead of the believing men and women.

studies.applyIt: Say one true thing today that costs you a little: an admission, a correction, a number you have been rounding in your own favour. Small is fine. The rank named in this ayah rests on a word for truthfulness that has become habitual, and habits are built out of instances that were slightly inconvenient at the time.

studies.title: Green, Then Yellow, Then Straw
studies.meaning: Worldly life is broken into five words that map a life in order. Play, then diversion, then ornament, then boasting, then piling up wealth and children. Early scholars read them as the sequence of a human being from childhood to old age. The parable that follows is from farming and moves fast: rain, growth that delights the farmers, yellowing, then broken straw. The instruction after it is not to withdraw but to race. The finish line named first is forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the second half of a surah pressing a community to spend on what was in front of it. The ayat just before describe men and women lending God a loan, and the ayat just after remove both grief and elation over what a person holds. Medina at this point had wealth it had not had before. No specific occasion is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: The root means to cover, and the classical readers take the word here in its agricultural sense: those who cover seed with soil. The same root gives the word for one who covers over truth.
Named from a verb meaning to smash. It is what remains of a crop after it dries and is trodden, useful only as fodder, and it is the last stage in a sequence the ayah runs at speed.
A reciprocal imperative from the verb for outstripping. The passage that has just called the world a game answers it with a race, so competition is redirected rather than condemned.
From a root for tricking someone into a bad bargain. The word does not say the enjoyment is unreal; it says the estimate of it is wrong, which is a narrower and harder claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming in Medina depended on a short window. Rain came, barley came up green, and within weeks the crop was either harvested or standing yellow in the field. Everyone had watched a field go from the best thing they had seen that year to stubble in the space of a season. The parable is not a metaphor a listener had to work at; it was last spring.
studies.didYouKnow: The garden is measured here by width rather than by contents. The measure given is the heavens and the earth together. Only one other passage in the Quran describes it that way. The comparison is useless as a quantity, on purpose. It takes the largest thing a listener can picture and uses it for the width alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not deny that the world is enjoyable. It denies that the enjoyment is what it looks like, which leaves the pleasures intact and removes their claim to be the point. Then it does something unusual: instead of asking for detachment it asks for speed, and the goal is put in the same competitive vocabulary the previous ayah used for boasting and accumulation. The drive is not removed. Its object is changed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction and the same measurement, in a surah about a battle rather than about wealth.
Runs the identical parable of rain and withered growth, calling worldly life by the same short life cycle.
Takes one item from this list, the piling up of more, and makes a whole surah of it.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own week and decide which of the five words it mostly belonged to: play, diversion, appearance, comparison, or accumulation. Do not moralise the answer. The list is descriptive, and every one of them is a normal part of a life. Then put one thing in next week that would not fit any of the five.
studies.explainEasier: Life in this world is play, show, bragging and piling up money and children. It is like rain that makes plants grow. Then they turn yellow and break into dry bits. So race towards God's forgiveness and a Garden as wide as the sky and earth.

studies.title: Written Before It Happens
studies.meaning: Two places are named where a misfortune can land, the earth and yourselves, and one clause covers both. Nothing strikes except that it is in a record before We bring it into being. Commentators discuss what the pronoun refers to, some reading it as the misfortune and some as the earth and the souls, and the range is left open. The closing line refuses to make any of it impressive: that is easy for God. The purpose of the whole statement arrives in the ayah after it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a surah addressed to people who had recently lost a great deal and recently gained a great deal. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. It sits between the parable of a crop that yellows and a statement about not grieving over losses or exulting over gains, so it is placed as a premise rather than as a doctrine offered for its own sake.

keyTerms.gloss: a misfortune, a thing that strikes
keyTerms.note: From a verb for hitting a target. The word describes an event by its accuracy rather than by its size, so a small setback and a bereavement are named with the same term.

A verb for originating something and separating it out, which gives one of the divine names for the Maker. Its precision matters, since the record is said to precede the making rather than the striking.
An ordinary adjective for something requiring no effort, from a root also used of small amounts. The claim is deliberately understated, which is how the Quran usually closes statements of this kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loss in that world arrived without warning and without explanation. A caravan failed to return, a well went dry, a child died in a season of fever. There was no insurance and no appeal, and the usual response was to read the event as luck, which the Arabs before Islam took seriously and attached to days and to the flight of birds. This ayah replaces luck with a record.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for bringing something into being is the root behind one of the divine names, the Originator, which appears in a run of three such names near the end of surah 59. The ayah therefore places the record earlier than the very act that name describes, which is the point the wording is making.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The statement is not offered as a solution to suffering and the chapter does not use it as one. What it does is remove surprise, and the next ayah says exactly what that is for: so that you do not grieve over what escaped you or exult over what you were given. Foreknowledge is put to work on the emotional life rather than on the philosophical question, which is why the Quran can state it so briefly and move on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the purpose of this statement directly, neither sorrow over a loss nor elation over a gain.
Says nothing befalls us except what God has decreed, and makes reliance on Him the conclusion.
Attaches the same idea to the heart, saying whoever believes has his heart guided through it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that went wrong this year and write one sentence about it with no explanation in it. Just what happened, when, and to whom. Most accounts of a loss are largely explanation. The ayah offers a different frame, and the first step in testing it is seeing the event without the story you have built around it.

studies.title: Neither Grief Nor Exultation
studies.meaning: The clause opens with a purpose particle. That attaches it to the ayah before, about everything being written down beforehand. Knowing in advance is given as the reason for a steady heart. Not indifference, but the removal of two exact reactions: grief at a loss and elation at a gain. Then two kinds of person are named as what that steadiness prevents. The one who struts, and the one who withholds and urges others to withhold.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah addressed to a community that had lately come into property and standing. The passage follows a statement that every misfortune on earth and in the self is written down before it happens. No particular occasion is reported. Arrogance and meanness are paired here for a reason. In that society a man's giving was public, and holding back was noticed and copied.

keyTerms.note: A verb for sorrow that settles rather than for a burst of it. The negation is of the lasting kind, so the sentence does not rule out feeling a loss; it addresses what a person does with it afterwards.
From a root connected with imagination and with horses. It describes a walk, someone moving as if watched, so the fault is named by a posture rather than by a belief.
Holding back what is due rather than merely being careful with money. The ayah adds a second stage, recommending it to others, which turns a private habit into something a community catches.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Arabia was built on giving. A man who slaughtered for guests in a lean year was remembered in verse; a man who did not was remembered too. Poets were paid to praise generosity and paid more to mock its absence, so meanness was not a private matter. And fortunes turned fast: a caravan lost, a season without rain, and a household's standing changed within a month.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 57 belongs to a group of five chapters. Each opens by saying everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God. Within it, this ayah is one of the few in the Quran that gives a reason for a feeling rather than for an action. The reason offered is a fact about record-keeping in the ayah before.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The written decree is used here for a practical purpose, not an abstract one. The point of a written record is not to settle a question about freedom. It is to change how a person holds a gain or a loss. That is an unusual move. The teaching is introduced and at once given a job. The two failures named afterwards show what is at stake. Both pride and meanness rest on believing that what you hold is yours by achievement.

crossReferences.why: Carries the statement this passage is attached to, that every event is recorded before it occurs.
Uses the identical pair of words for the strutting boaster, this time inside a father's advice to his son.
Repeats the same two-stage description of meanness, holding back and then urging others to hold back.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you lost this year and something you gained, and write one sentence about each in the same flat tone, as if reporting on someone else. That evenness is what the ayah is describing. It is not a feeling you can summon, but the writing exercise gets you close enough to notice the difference.
studies.explainEasier: God writes down what will happen before it does. Knowing this helps people not to be crushed by what they lose or puffed up by what they get. God does not love people who show off or hold back what they should give.

studies.title: The Book, The Balance, The Iron
studies.meaning: Three things are described as sent down and the third is the surprise. Messengers came with clear proofs, and with them the Book and the balance, so that people would stand in fairness. And We sent down iron, in which is great force and benefits for people. Commentators read the sending down of iron as its being made available rather than as a physical descent, and note that the ayah gives it two properties without ranking them. The purpose clause that follows is about knowing who supports God unseen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period when the community had responsibilities it had not carried before. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. It gives the chapter its name, and the naming is unusual: this is the only surah in the Quran titled after a metal, in a Book whose chapter names are usually drawn from a story, an animal or a divine attribute.

keyTerms.note: The word for a weighing instrument. Surah 55 uses the same term for a balance set beneath the raised sky, so the Quran applies it both to the order of the world and to what a messenger brings with him.

A word for a just share, distinguished by the lexicons from the general word for justice by its reference to portions. Standing in it is described as something people do rather than as something done to them.
The metal, named three times in the Quran and giving this chapter its title. The root also carries sharpness and limit, which is why the same letters give Arabic its word for a boundary.
A phrase for doing something where it cannot be observed. Attached to supporting God and His messengers, it makes the test one of conduct without an audience rather than of declared allegiance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Iron in Arabia came mostly from outside and was expensive. A sword was inherited, named and remembered, and a smith was a specialist a whole district depended on. The same metal made ploughshares, nails, cooking pots and knives. Everyone in the audience knew both halves of what this ayah says about it, because both came out of the same forge in the same week.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only chapter of the Quran named after a metal. Its title comes from one word in this ayah, and the word itself appears three times in the whole Book: here, in an account of a barrier built across a mountain pass, and in a statement about the metal being made soft in the hands of a prophet.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation and force are named in one sentence and neither is apologised for. The Book and the balance establish what fairness is; iron is what makes a standard enforceable and also what builds the tools of an ordinary life. The ayah gives it both properties in a single clause and does not separate them. What follows is the qualifier: the point of all three is to make visible who supports the arrangement when nobody is watching.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same balance beneath the sky and warns against transgressing in it or falling short of it.
Tells believers to stand firmly for fairness as witnesses, even against themselves or their parents.
Describes iron made soft for David and the making of armour, one of its three mentions in the Book.

studies.applyIt: Find the sharpest tool in your house and look at it properly: a kitchen knife, scissors, a blade in a drawer. It is useful and it is dangerous, and nothing about the object decides which. The ayah names both properties in one clause and then says the real test is what you do when nobody is watching.

studies.title: Noah, Abraham, And Their Line
studies.meaning: Two names stand for the whole history. Noah and Abraham were sent, and prophethood and the Book were placed in their descendants, so the line of revelation is described as running through a family rather than appearing at intervals. Then the outcome is given in one balanced clause: among them is one who is guided, and many of them break out of every bound. The same clause closes the ayah after this one, word for word, so the chapter passes its verdict on two eras in identical terms.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a passage placing the community it addresses inside a long sequence rather than at the start of one. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Naming Noah and Abraham together covers the whole span the audience recognised, since one stood at the beginning after the flood and the other was the ancestor claimed by the Arabs and by the communities they lived beside.

keyTerms.note: An abstract noun for the office rather than for a person, occurring five times in the Quran. Naming it as something placed in a line treats prophecy as an institution with a history, not only as a series of individual callings.
A dual possessive, so the descendants of the two are counted as one line. The word covers descendants at any distance, which is how a single term can span the many centuries the ayah is summarising.

From a root describing a date leaving its skin. It names stepping outside a boundary rather than denying anything, which is why the word can be applied to people inside a tradition rather than outside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the framework of everything in Arabia. A man was his lineage, alliances were marriages, and the tribes of the Hijaz traced themselves to Abraham and regarded the sanctuary at Mecca as his building. An audience hearing that prophethood had been placed in a line was not hearing an abstract claim about history but a statement about the family they said they belonged to.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one that follows end with exactly the same words, that many of them broke out of every bound. The chapter passes one verdict on two long eras without varying its wording, and the repetition is easy to miss on a first reading because the second ayah is more than twice the length of the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Inheritance of an office is affirmed and then immediately qualified. Prophethood and scripture run in a line, and the moral outcome does not: the ayah counts one guided among many who went outside the bounds. That combination cuts in two directions at once. It grants the line its standing, and it removes the idea that standing travels with the office, which matters for a community beginning to think of itself as an inheritance.

crossReferences.why: Says the same of Abraham, that prophethood and the Book were placed among his descendants.
Recalls that the Book and wisdom were given to the family of Abraham, along with a great kingdom.
Records the answer to Abraham's request for his line, that the covenant does not reach wrongdoers.

studies.applyIt: Name something you inherited that you have never actually taken up: a craft, a language, a practice, a habit of mind from a grandparent. Say out loud what it would cost to begin. The ayah is precise that a line can carry an office while most of the people in it stand outside what it asks, and knowing which you are is a question rather than a mood.

studies.title: Compassion, Mercy, And Monasticism
studies.meaning: Messengers followed one another, and then Jesus son of Mary, and the Gospel was given to him. What was put into the hearts of those who followed him is named as two things, tenderness and mercy. Then a third appears and it is described differently: a withdrawal from the world which they originated, which We did not prescribe for them, taken up in seeking God's approval. Commentators read that clause in more than one way, and they agree on what follows, that it was not kept as it should have been.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The chapter has placed its audience inside a long line of revelation and reaches the most recent link here. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Christian communities were known to the audience through the trade with Syria and Abyssinia and through monks living along the caravan routes, several of whom appear in the early accounts, so the practice described was something travellers had seen.

keyTerms.note: A verb for placing one thing behind another in a track, from the root for the back of the neck. It makes the sequence of messengers a single procession rather than a series of separate appearances.
The same two words the chapter used of God a few lines earlier. Here they describe what was placed in the hearts of the followers, so a divine pair is handed to human beings as a characteristic.
Found only here in the Quran, from a root for awe and fear. It names a way of life rather than an attitude, and the ayah presents it as something originated rather than as something sent down.
A verb for bringing something into existence without a precedent. The same root gives a divine name for the one who originates the heavens and the earth, so the word by itself carries no criticism.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Monks were a familiar sight on the Syrian road. They kept cells near the routes, gave water and shelter to travellers, and Arab merchants who ran the northern trade knew several of them by name. Their poverty and their solitude were understood and often admired. An audience in Medina had a specific picture in mind here rather than a category, which is why the ayah can treat the practice with such care.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the monastic life in this ayah appears once in the whole Quran. The verb used for taking it up means originating something without a precedent, and its root also gives one of the names of God as the Originator of the heavens and the earth, so the verb itself carries no reproach and the reproach in the line falls elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is unusually careful. It records what was given, names what was added, states that it was not prescribed, credits the motive as seeking God's approval, and then says it was not kept as it should have been. Each of those is a separate clause and none cancels the one before it. The ayah ends by giving the believers among them their reward, so the assessment separates a practice from the people who followed it.

crossReferences.why: Names priests and monks among those nearest in affection to the believers, and gives a reason for it.
Gives the announcement of Jesus son of Mary and his standing, which this ayah takes as known.
Describes the Gospel given to him, carrying guidance and light and confirming what came before it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you took on that nobody required of you: an extra hour of work each week, a rule about your phone, a promise to call someone regularly. Ask honestly whether you are still keeping it. The ayah is careful about exactly that distinction, crediting the intention and then noting that the thing was not observed as it should have been.

studies.title: A Double Share And A Light
studies.meaning: An address to believers asks two things and promises three. Be mindful of God, and believe in His Messenger: you will be given a double portion of His mercy, a light to walk by, and forgiveness. The word for the portion is a measure, and commentators discuss the doubling at length, most reading it as a share for what came before and a share for what has come now. The light returns from earlier in the chapter, and this time the verb attached to it is walking rather than running ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah follows the passage about the earlier communities and is usually read together with the line after it, which addresses the People of the Book directly. No specific occasion is reported for it. Medina had long-established scriptural communities living alongside the new one, and the chapter's closing lines treat the relation between them in terms of grace rather than of history.

keyTerms.note: A dual from a word for a measured share, found in this form only here. Its singular is used elsewhere in the Quran for a share of responsibility, so the same measure covers a burden and a reward.
The same light the chapter showed running ahead on the day of reckoning, given here with a verb for ordinary walking. The reward is described as usable now rather than only at the end.

From a root for putting a shield between yourself and harm. It describes an ongoing care rather than a single act, which is why it is paired here with a verb for believing rather than with a verb for doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A share in Arabia was a measured thing. Spoils were divided into portions, inheritance was counted in fractions, and water at a well was allotted by turns. Everyone knew what it meant to be given a double share of something, and it was a public honour rather than a private benefit. Promising a doubled portion used the language of a distribution people had watched being made.
studies.didYouKnow: The dual word for a double portion in this ayah occurs only here. Its singular appears elsewhere in the Quran for the share of responsibility that comes from intervening in an affair, whether for good or for ill, so the same measure is used in the Book both for what you gain and for what you end up carrying.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three gifts are named and only one of them belongs to the hereafter. The light is for walking now, and the forgiveness is given without any condition beyond the two verbs at the head of the line. That makes the ayah an offer rather than a warning, which is where the chapter chooses to end its argument after twenty-seven lines of pressing and rebuking. The last words given to the reader are two divine names.

crossReferences.why: Promises a double reward to those given scripture before who then believed and were patient.
Develops the same image of light at much greater length, light upon light, given to whom God wills.
Shows the light promised here in its later form, running ahead on the day of reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you carry as a burden and one thing you count as a gain, and notice that you use different language for each. This ayah uses the same measure word for both. Spend a minute holding them in a single sentence, as two portions of one allotment, and see whether either of them changes size.

studies.title: Grace Is In God's Hand
studies.meaning: The chapter's last line explains the one before it, and it does so with a construction the grammarians discuss at length, since a negative particle sits where the sense does not appear to need one. Commentators read it as emphasis rather than as denial, and take the meaning as: so that the People of the Book may know that they have no power at all over God's grace. Then the positive statement, twice over. Grace is in God's hand, He gives it to whom He wills, and He is the possessor of immense grace.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a surah that has moved from the names of God through spending, through hypocrisy, and through the history of revelation. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. Medina contained long-established scriptural communities and a new one, and questions about which had a claim on divine favour were live, so the chapter ends on the general principle rather than on any particular dispute.

keyTerms.note: A construction the grammarians treat as carrying an extra negative particle for emphasis, a known feature of classical Arabic. The commentators read the phrase positively, and the discussion of it fills pages in the older works.
A verb for being able to determine or measure something out. Denying it here says that no group can allocate God's favour, which is a statement about capacity rather than about anyone's worth.
A noun for what exceeds what is due. The word appears three times in this single ayah, each time in a different construction, which is why the line reads as a conclusion rather than as a fresh claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Favour in Arabia was distributed by people with names. A chief's patronage, a merchant's credit, a clan's protection: each was allocated by somebody who could be petitioned and who could refuse. The whole social world ran on knowing whose hand a benefit had come from. This closing line takes the word for that kind of favour and names one hand as the source of all of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for grace appears three times in this single ayah and in three different positions: as something nobody can control, as something held in God's hand, and as an attribute of God Himself. The chapter's very last word is the same adjective it used earlier for the great triumph promised to the believers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah ends by removing the question of entitlement rather than by answering it. No community is said to be able to reach God's favour and none is said to be excluded; the capacity to allocate is denied to everybody. That leaves grace as something given rather than earned or held, which matches how the chapter opened, where six lines of description came before the first request. What began by establishing scale ends by saying the scale is not administered by anyone in the room.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle, that God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, in a similar setting.
Says the grace is in God's hand and that He gives it to whom He wills, in almost the same words.
Calls it the grace of God given to whom He wills, and names Him the possessor of immense grace.

studies.applyIt: Think of one advantage you have that you did not arrange: where you were born, a language you grew up in, a person who took an interest in you early. Name it plainly, without gratitude language, as a fact about allocation. The chapter closes on exactly that point, and the exercise works better as an observation than as a feeling.
